query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the fraction of an oxide‐forming element in high‐entropy alloy coatings will promote the in situ formation of a robust nanocrystalline oxide tribolayer during wear at elevated temperatures, which in turn reduces wear by serving as a self-adjusting friction modifier.
generation.material_initial_state: A multiphase, multi‐element HEA coating with a baseline low concentration of a key oxide‐forming element.
generation.intervention: Increase the fraction of the oxide‐forming element (e.g., Ti or Al) by 10–20% relative to the baseline composition.
generation.conditions: Wear testing under controlled sliding contact at temperatures between 500–900 °C in an atmospheric environment that permits oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: The dynamic, nanocrystalline oxide tribolayer (e.g., a spinel or similar protective oxide phase) formed in situ during wear.
generation.mechanism: A higher content of the oxide‐forming element enhances the formation and stability of the protective oxide layer during wear, which minimizes direct metal contact and thereby reduces the wear rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline, coatings with increased oxide-former content will exhibit a thicker, more continuous tribolayer, lower wear rates, and a slightly reduced coefficient of friction.
generation.baseline: HEA coatings with a lower concentration of the oxide‐forming element, which form thinner or less stable tribolayers and consequently exhibit higher wear rates.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to hold under elevated temperatures (500–900 °C) in atmospheres that allow oxidation; environments outside these conditions (e.g., non-oxidizing or extremely high temperature conditions) might not produce the anticipated tribolayer behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal increase in the oxide-former concentration and the precise structural details governing tribolayer adhesion and thickness require further experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of HEA coatings: one with a baseline oxide-former content and one with a 10–20% increased oxide-former content. Subject both sets to identical sliding wear tests at elevated temperatures (500–900 °C) in air.
measurements: Quantitative wear rate (via mass or volume loss measurements)
Characterization of the surface layer (using SEM/EDS and/or XRD) to assess tribolayer thickness and continuity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coatings with increased oxide-former content do not show a statistically significant reduction in wear rate, fail to produce a more robust tribolayer, or if wear performance deteriorates relative to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . occupying_moves.technique: pin‐on‐disk tribometry combined with in situ surface/phase characterization (e.g., SEM/EBSD)
occupying_moves.conditions: Systematic variation of key elemental fractions (e.g., increasing/reducing elements that drive the formation of protective oxide or strain‐induced hard phases) under standardized wear loads and speeds relevant to protective coatings

chosen.technique: pin‐on‐disk wear testing integrated with in situ microscopy and surface phase analysis
chosen.conditions: Testing a series of high-entropy alloy coatings with controlled variations in elements predicted to control tribolayer formation (e.g., by emphasizing oxide-forming components) under wear-relevant loads and speeds (ambient to moderate elevated temperature) to delineate the effect of composition on the formation and stability of a protective phase
chosen.why: This move directly addresses the open question by isolating the role of composition in governing wear behavior. By controlling the alloy composition to promote or suppress protective tribolayer/phase formation and coupling wear testing with in situ characterization, the study can test whether a mechanistic link exists between the induced microstructural changes and the wear performance. This approach reflects standard experimental studies in the field and is robust in distinguishing the hypothesis from a baseline alloy lacking the controlled compositional intervention.

frame.system: High‐entropy alloy (HEA) protective coatings used for wear-resistant applications. The starting state is a multiphase, multi‐element coating system where the interactions between constituent elements during wear are not fully established.
frame.goal: To develop a mechanistic understanding of how wear performance is governed in HEA coatings through controlled formation and stability of a nanocrystalline tribolayer (e.g., an oxide or mechanically mixed layer) that mitigates wear.
frame.limitation: The absence of a single, testable hypothesis linking compositional tuning to the dynamic evolution of protective tribolayers under wear conditions, limiting predictive and design capabilities.
root_cause_cues: range over which it should hold
constraints: Must propose one single testable mechanistic hypothesis
Clearly define a controlled compositional change (e.g., addition or removal of an element that stabilizes the oxide/trilayer)
Must state expected directional observations relative to the baseline
Identify the operational range (e.g., temperature, sliding speed, compositional variation)
Must include evidence from past observations and a falsification criterion
frame.regime: Testing within simulated wear conditions such as sliding contact at elevated temperatures where tribological interactions (e.g., oxidation, plastic flow) occur. Environmental factors (ambient air or controlled atmosphere) that enable or inhibit oxide formation should be considered.
prior_attempts: Empirical wear tests correlating overall composition with wear rate without isolating the role of in situ formed tribolayers
Comparative studies that varied composition but did not control for the dynamic evolution of nanostructured surface phases during wear
frame.understanding: The hypothesis posits that the wear performance of HEA coatings is primarily governed by the controlled formation and stability of a dynamic, nanocrystalline tribolayer, which acts as a self-adjusting friction modifier. Specifically, by intentionally varying the concentration of elements known to form stable oxides under wear conditions, one can induce more robust tribolayer formation. This would be evidenced by reduced wear rates compared to baseline compositions, a distinct non‐linear relationship between the adding element concentration and wear performance, and consistent behavior over a specified temperature and sliding speed range. A falsification observation would be the absence of a measurable tribolayer or an opposite trend (i.e., increased wear with the modification), thereby undermining the hypothesized mechanism.

decision.trend: Early studies on HEA wear behavior focused on overall composition–wear rate correlations without isolating the in situ evolution of nanostructured surface layers. For example, PMC7515071 showed that under reciprocating wear at elevated temperatures the formation of a spinel phase is associated with improved wear performance, hinting that tribolayer formation matters. Later work such as PMC7304825, while emphasizing processing routes and post-deposition treatments, confirmed that nanocrystalline film microstructure and surface phase evolution (e.g., through annealing) can influence tribological performance. In both cases, the evolution of a protective tribolayer under wear conditions emerged as an important, yet not definitively isolated, factor.
decision.unsolved: A direct, testable mechanistic link between controlled compositional adjustments and the dynamic formation/stability of protective nanocrystalline tribolayers has not been established. In particular, it remains unclear how tuning the concentration of specific oxide‐forming elements (which drive the tribolayer formation) governs wear performance under conditions relevant to HEA protective coatings.
decision.lever: alloy composition (specifically, the fraction of a key oxide‐forming element such as Ti or Al)
decision.why: Given the trend that improved wear resistance at high temperature correlates with the in situ formation of a protective spinel or similar oxide phase, the next logical step is to perform a systematic experiment in which the concentration of an oxide‐forming element is varied relative to a baseline composition. This approach directly addresses the gap by isolating the influence of elemental composition on tribolayer formation, predicting a non‐linear improvement in wear performance when the oxide former is increased within a key operational range (e.g., 500–900 °C under sliding contact). Such an experiment would yield the controlled change, expected directional observations, and falsification criteria needed to establish a single, testable mechanistic hypothesis linking composition to dynamic tribolayer stability during wear.
